To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the 32 bp-deleted allele of the CCR 5 gene (delta c cr 5) is associated in heterozygotes with lower plasma HIV-1 RNA levels and higher percentages of total CD4+T lymphocytes in perinally infected children at a median age of eight years.

the 32-bp CCR5 mutation was associated with significantly lower virus loads, higher CD4 T cell counts, and a trend for lower progression rates to AIDS (CDC C) in a cohort of children with perinatal HIV infection.

the presence of a 32-bp CCR5 deletion allele in perinatall HIV-infected children is associated with lower virus load and better CD4 cell counts at 8 years, but not with higher HIV-specific cytotoxic CD8 T cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of CCR5 in the pathogenesis of HIV in children.
the study of the role of the CCR-5 delta 32 mutation in the natural history of HIV infection.
understanding the mechanisms of the immune responses to human immunodeficiency type 1 ( HIV-1 ) infection in children.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the CCR5 delta 32 allele is not a protective allele for HIV-1 disease progression in children.
the CCR5 delta 32 allele is associated with a reduced HIV-1 disease progression in children and that this effect is due to a reduction in HIV-1 plasma viremia.
the CCR5 delta32 allele has a protective effect on HIV disease progression in children.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the CCR5 delta32 allele confers a selective advantage against HIV-1 infection in heterozygotes.
the CCR5 delta32 mutation is a marker of a more favorable course of HIV disease in perinatall infected children.
the CCR5 3' 32-bp deleted allele has a protective effect on plasma HIV-1 RNA load, and on CD4 T-cell counts in perinatallly HIV-1 infected children.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we found a significant impact of the CCR 5 delta 32 heterozygosity on the virologic and immune status of perinatally infected children.
we can use this genetic marker to predict the course of HIV infection in children, but not in adults.
CCR5 is a major coreceptor for HIV and that CCR5 deficiency is a major factor in the control of HIV infection.
